Bill and Flipper Morphology of Palmer Archipelago Penguins

A Quarto report exploring body size relationships across three penguin species

Author

Yang An

Published

September 29, 2026

Introduction

This report revisits the penguins dataset from the palmerpenguins package, which has already been used earlier in this course to explore flipper length and body mass. Here the focus shifts to a relationship we have not yet looked at closely: how bill length and flipper length relate to one another across the three species recorded at the Palmer Long-Term Ecological Research station in Antarctica – Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo penguins.

The goals of this report are to:

  • clean the data and remove any incomplete records,
  • summarize body size by species and sex in a clean, readable table, and
  • visualize the relationship between bill length and flipper length with a publication-quality figure.

Data Preparation

Before summarizing or plotting anything, the raw penguins data are cleaned. Rows with missing measurements or unrecorded sex are dropped so that every summary statistic below is calculated from complete cases only. This keeps the table and the figure consistent with one another.

Code 
# Drop any row with a missing value in the columns we actually use.
# This avoids NA-driven warnings later and keeps the table and the
# figure based on an identical set of individuals.
penguins_clean <- penguins |>
  drop_na(bill_length_mm, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g, sex) |>
  mutate(
    species = as.factor(species),
    sex = as.factor(sex)
  )

After cleaning, the dataset contains 333 penguins (out of 344 originally recorded), spread across three species and two islands of observation.

Summary Table

Table 1 below reports the mean bill length, mean flipper length, and sample size for each combination of species and sex. Grouping by both variables shows that, within every species, males tend to have slightly longer bills and flippers than females – a pattern worth keeping in mind before interpreting the scatter plot in the next section.

Code 
penguin_summary <- penguins_clean |>
  group_by(species, sex) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_bill_length_mm = round(mean(bill_length_mm), 1),
    mean_flipper_length_mm = round(mean(flipper_length_mm), 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# kableExtra turns the plain summary table into a styled HTML table:
# striped rows, a bolded header, and hover-highlighting make it easy
# to read on screen.
penguin_summary |>
  kbl(
    col.names = c("Species", "Sex", "n", "Mean Bill Length (mm)",
                  "Mean Flipper Length (mm)"),
    align = "c"
  ) |>
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
    full_width = FALSE
  ) |>
  row_spec(0, bold = TRUE, color = "white", background = "#0072B2")
Table 1: Mean bill length and flipper length (mm) by species and sex, with sample sizes.
Species Sex n Mean Bill Length (mm) Mean Flipper Length (mm)
Adelie female 73 37.3 187.8
Adelie male 73 40.4 192.4
Chinstrap female 34 46.6 191.7
Chinstrap male 34 51.1 199.9
Gentoo female 58 45.6 212.7
Gentoo male 61 49.5 221.5

Visualizing the Relationship

Figure 1 shows bill length plotted against flipper length for every penguin in the cleaned dataset, colored by species. A few design choices were made deliberately, following best practices covered in lecture:

  1. Color-blind-safe palette. The three species are distinguished using the Okabe-Ito palette (#0072B2, #D55E00, #009E73), which remains distinguishable for the most common forms of color vision deficiency.
  2. Linear trend lines per species, added with geom_smooth(), make the within-species relationship easy to see even though the species overlap in places.
  3. Clear, fully-labeled axes and a legend title, so the figure can stand alone without needing the surrounding text.
Code 
ggplot(penguins_clean, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = bill_length_mm,
                            color = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
    "Adelie" = "#0072B2",
    "Chinstrap" = "#D55E00",
    "Gentoo" = "#009E73"
  )) +
  labs(
    title = "Bill Length vs. Flipper Length in Palmer Penguins",
    subtitle = "Each species shows a positive within-species relationship",
    x = "Flipper Length (mm)",
    y = "Bill Length (mm)",
    color = "Species"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "grey30"),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

Gentoo penguins (green) separate out clearly as the largest-bodied species, with the longest flippers and comparatively long bills, while Adelie and Chinstrap penguins overlap more in flipper length but remain distinguishable by bill length.

Conclusion

Both the table and the figure tell a consistent story: body size in this dataset is not one-dimensional. Flipper length and bill length both increase together within each species, but the three species occupy different regions of that relationship – meaning either measurement alone would be enough to make a reasonable guess at species identity for most individuals. The full, reproducible workflow behind both outputs (data cleaning, summarizing, and plotting) is documented in the code chunks above.
